Treat the three universal claims independently; the displayed `Iff` holds simply because both sides are always true.

For the first conjunct, show that the \(p\) powers \(1,\zeta,\ldots,\zeta^{p-1}\) exhaust the roots of \(X^p-1\). Primitivity makes these powers distinct, while the domain assumption bounds the number of roots by the polynomial’s degree. Thus \(\eta_1=\zeta^r\) and \(\eta_2=\zeta^s\). Since \(\zeta-1\mid \zeta^m-1\) for every \(m\), it divides
\[
(\eta_1-1)-(\eta_2-1)=\eta_1-\eta_2.
\]

For the left side of the `Iff`, factor
\[
\zeta^{i+j}-\zeta^i=\zeta^i(\zeta^j-1).
\]
The factor \(\zeta^i\) is a unit. Coprimality of \(j\) and \(n\) supplies an inverse of \(j\) modulo \(n\), so geometric-series factorizations give divisibility both ways between \(\zeta^j-1\) and \(\zeta-1\). Domain cancellation, together with \(n\ge2\) and primitivity ensuring \(\zeta-1\ne0\), shows the corresponding quotient is a unit; hence the two differences are associated.

For the right side, induct on \(k\), using the standard GCD-monoid inequality
\[
\gcd(a,xy)\mid \gcd(a,x)\,\gcd(a,y).
\]
With \(x=b^k\) and \(y=b\), the induction hypothesis yields
\[
\gcd(a,b^{k+1})
 \mid \gcd(a,b^k)\gcd(a,b)
 \mid \gcd(a,b)^{k+1}.
\]
After proving these two unrelated universal statements, conclude their equivalence by truth on both sides.
